definition: Cookies created by websites other than the one you're currently visiting, typically used for cross-site tracking, advertising, and analytics purposes.
metaDescription: Learn about third-party cookies, how they track you across websites, and why major browsers are phasing them out for better privacy protection.
simpleExplanation: When you visit a website, it might load content from other companies (like ads or social media buttons). These other companies can place cookies on your browser to track your activity across multiple websites, building a profile of your interests.
whyItMatters: Third-party cookies enable extensive cross-site tracking, allowing advertisers and data brokers to build detailed profiles of your browsing habits without your explicit consent, raising significant privacy concerns.
technicalDetail: Third-party cookies are set by domains different from the one in your address bar. They're embedded through iframes, scripts, or resources from external domains. Modern browsers are implementing policies like SameSite=None requirements and eventually blocking them entirely to enhance user privacy.

examples.explanation: You look at shoes on one website, then visit a news site and see ads for those exact shoes. A third-party cookie from an ad network tracked you across both sites.
Facebook's Like button on various websites uses third-party cookies to track your browsing even when you don't click it, building a profile of sites you visit.
Google Analytics uses third-party cookies to track user behavior across different websites that use their service, providing cross-site user journey data.
